notice: RN bank batch 32: Mental health I: communication, anxiety, crisis and grief. Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: A client says, "I'm worthless. Nobody cares about me." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: "You're feeling that you have no value to anyone?"

rationale.correct: Therapeutic techniques: reflecting, restating, open-ended questions, silence and clarifying.

perOption.a: Reflecting the feeling invites the client to explore it.
perOption.b: This is false reassurance and dismisses the feeling.
perOption.c: 'Why' questions can feel judgmental and make the client defensive.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which statement by a nurse is a nontherapeutic communication technique?

rationale.correct: Avoid false reassurance, advice-giving, 'why' questions, changing the subject and judgment.

perOption.a: This is an open-ended prompt.
perOption.b: False reassurance blocks discussion of feelings.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client asks the nurse, "Are you married? Do you have kids?" What is the best response?

options.text: "We're here to focus on you. Tell me how your day has been."
Share personal details to build trust

rationale.correct: Keep the therapeutic relationship focused on the client.

perOption.a: This redirects to the client and keeps professional boundaries.
perOption.b: This shifts the focus away from the client.
perOption.c: This is rude and damages rapport.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client says, "I'll tell you something if you promise not to tell anyone." What is the best response?

options.text: "I can't promise that. If it affects your safety or care, I'll need to share it with the team."

rationale.correct: Information that affects safety must be shared with the treatment team.

perOption.a: Nurses can't keep secrets that involve safety, such as suicidal plans.
perOption.b: The nurse may have to break this promise.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a request for secrecy.

questions.stem: A client is having a panic attack, breathing fast and saying, "I'm going to die." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stay with the client, speak calmly and use short, simple sentences
Teach the client about panic disorder
Leave the client alone to calm down
Ask the client why they're panicking

rationale.correct: Severe or panic anxiety: stay, stay calm, simple directions, reduce stimulation.

perOption.a: In panic, the client can't process complex information; presence lowers anxiety.
perOption.b: Teaching isn't possible during panic.
perOption.c: The client shouldn't be left alone.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with generalized anxiety disorder is starting buspirone. Which statement shows correct understanding?

options.text: "It may take a few weeks before I notice a difference."
"I'll take it only when I feel anxious."
"It will make me very sleepy right away."

rationale.correct: Buspirone: scheduled dosing, delayed effect, little sedation or dependence.

perOption.a: Buspirone's effects build over 2 to 4 weeks.
perOption.b: It is taken on a schedule.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed lorazepam for short-term anxiety. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I won't drink alcohol while taking this."
"I'll stop it suddenly when I feel better."
"I won't drive until I know how it affects me."

rationale.correct: Benzodiazepines: avoid alcohol, taper off, watch for sedation and dependence.

perOption.a: Alcohol adds to CNS depression.
perOption.b: Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal and seizures.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A newly admitted client with OCD washes their hands for 30 minutes before every meal and is often late. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Allow time for the ritual and plan the schedule around it
Make the client skip meals if late
Point out that the behavior is irrational

rationale.correct: OCD: early on, allow rituals, then gradually limit them while teaching coping skills.

perOption.a: Stopping rituals abruptly raises anxiety; limits are set gradually later.
perOption.b: This sharply increases anxiety.
perOption.d: The client already knows; this doesn't help.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for a client with OCD.

questions.stem: A veteran startles easily, has nightmares and avoids crowded places after combat. Which disorder do these findings suggest?

rationale.correct: PTSD: intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood and hyperarousal; use trauma-informed care.

perOption.a: Hyperarousal, re-experiencing and avoidance after trauma are typical of PTSD.
perOption.b: GAD isn't tied to a trauma.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate the defense mechanism it shows.

rows.text: A client diagnosed with diabetes keeps eating sweets and says, "I don't really have diabetes."
A client who is angry says to the nurse, "You're angry with me."
After being yelled at by the boss, a client goes home and yells at the dog
A student who failed an exam says, "The test was unfair anyway."

rationale.correct: Recognize common defense mechanisms in client statements.

perOption.r1:c1: Refusing to accept reality is denial.
perOption.r1:c2: No feelings are attributed to others.
perOption.r2:c2: The client attributes their own feelings to the nurse.
perOption.r2:c3: The feeling isn't shifted to a safer target.
perOption.r3:c3: Anger is shifted to a safer target.
perOption.r4:c4: A plausible excuse is given for the failure.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client arrives in crisis after losing a job and home. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Whether the client has thoughts of harming self or others

rationale.correct: Crisis intervention: ensure safety, focus on the immediate problem, use coping strategies and supports.

perOption.a: Safety is the first priority in crisis.
perOption.b: This isn't the focus of crisis intervention.
perOption.c: Crisis work focuses on the present.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a terminal illness says, "If I can just live until my daughter's wedding, I'll be ready." Which stage of grief does this reflect?

rationale.correct: Kübler-Ross stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance (not always in order).

perOption.a: Bargaining is trying to make a deal for more time.
perOption.b: The client acknowledges the illness.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two weeks after her husband died, a client cries often, has trouble sleeping and still eats regular meals. How should the nurse interpret this?

rationale.correct: Support normal grief; watch for prolonged, disabling grief or suicidal thoughts.

perOption.a: Sadness and sleep changes are expected early in grief.
perOption.b: It's too early to label this, and she's functioning.
perOption.c: This is diagnosed when grief is prolonged and disabling.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client asks to have a traditional healer visit in addition to medical treatment. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Support the request and coordinate with the team so the practices don't interfere with treatment
Tell the client this isn't allowed
Tell the client to stop medical treatment

rationale.correct: Culturally responsive care includes safe traditional practices.

perOption.a: Respecting cultural practices supports trust and adherence.
perOption.b: This disregards cultural values.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client says, "I feel like God has abandoned me." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Listen, explore the client's feelings and offer to contact the chaplain or a spiritual leader
Share the nurse's own religious beliefs
Tell the client those feelings are wrong

rationale.correct: Assess spiritual needs and refer according to the client's wishes.

perOption.a: This addresses spiritual distress respectfully.
perOption.b: This dismisses the client.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: After a stressful event, a client suddenly can't move the right arm, even though tests are normal, and seems unconcerned. What does this suggest?

rationale.correct: Conversion disorder: real symptoms without an organic cause, linked to stress; avoid focusing on the symptom.

perOption.a: Neurologic symptoms without an organic cause, often with indifference, suggest conversion.
perOption.b: The tests are normal.
perOption.c: Symptoms aren't intentionally produced in conversion.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which treatment is most effective for a specific phobia of dogs?

rationale.correct: Phobias respond to exposure-based behavioral therapy.

perOption.a: Gradual exposure reduces fear.
perOption.b: This maintains the fear.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: During a private screening, a client says her partner hits her. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess her immediate safety and help her develop a safety plan
Tell her she must leave her partner today
Confront the partner in the waiting room
Document it and take no other action

rationale.correct: IPV: screen privately, believe the client, assess safety, create a safety plan and give resources.

perOption.a: Safety comes first, and the client decides on next steps.
perOption.b: Leaving can be the most dangerous time; the client decides.
perOption.d: Safety planning and resources are needed.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to disclosure of intimate partner violence.

questions.stem: A client says that after the beatings, her partner apologizes, brings gifts and promises it won't happen again. Which phase of the cycle of violence is this?

rationale.correct: Cycle of violence: tension building, then acute battering, then honeymoon, then repeat.

perOption.a: Remorse and affection follow the battering.
perOption.b: This involves increasing stress and minor incidents.
perOption.d: This isn't a phase of the cycle.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client calls after being sexually assaulted an hour ago. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Please don't shower, change clothes or brush your teeth before coming in."
"Take a shower to feel better first."

rationale.correct: Sexual assault: preserve evidence, give prompt care (ideally a SANE exam) and offer support and prophylaxis.

perOption.a: This preserves evidence.
perOption.b: This destroys evidence.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach evidence preservation after sexual assault.

questions.stem: A client says, "My son never visits me anymore." Select the 2 most therapeutic responses.

options.text: "You're feeling hurt that your son doesn't visit?"
"Tell me more about your relationship with your son."

rationale.correct: Reflection and open-ended questions encourage clients to share feelings.

perOption.a: Reflecting the feeling is therapeutic.
perOption.b: An open-ended prompt encourages expression.
perOption.c: This is false reassurance and minimizes the feeling.
perOption.e: This shifts the focus to the nurse.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
